thresholds_comment: Mutation testing for the API package. §2 of the engineering spec sets an 85% kill rate as the target. `break` is 85 for a direct `npx stryker run`, which mutates the whole API (a day of runner time). The nightly does not run that: scripts/mutation-slice.mjs mutates one slice of twenty and writes a config for it whose `break` is the slice's own floor from scripts/mutation-slices.json (its measured score minus a point), so the job fails when that slice gets worse, not because the target is missed. `high`/`low` only colour the report. Stryker treats any `<option>_comment` key as documentation and ignores it.
ignoreStatic_comment: A static mutant sits in code that runs when a module loads (a top-level constant, a lookup table, a decorator argument), so no single test reaches it and Stryker runs the whole suite for it. In the 20-slice run of 2026-11-02 (workflow run 41454768502) they were 1–12% of a slice's mutants and 42–94% of its test time (Stryker's own warning, typically about three quarters), which is why slices of the same mutant count took 21 to over 95 minutes. They are not run: the report lists them as Ignored and they count neither as killed nor as survived, so the score is the score of the mutants a test can reach. Stryker documents the option for this reason. What it gives up is the constants and tables no test can be pointed at; the number of ignored mutants is in each slice's report.
ignorePatterns_comment: Stryker copies the project into .stryker-tmp before mutating. In this monorepo an unrestricted sandbox tries to copy optimization-engine/.venv (138M), web/node_modules (439M) and mobile/node_modules (169M) — it never finishes. This whitelist keeps the sandbox to what the API package actually needs to run its unit tests. If a new top-level file becomes a test dependency, add it here or the run fails with a missing-module error. After nest-cli.json come the files unit specs read from outside src/: contract specs that hold the gateway to the migrations, the web's messages and the app's types. Each entry is read by a spec Stryker runs, and without it that spec fails (checked by moving each out of the sandbox in turn): prisma/migrations/**/migration.sql (admin-areas, access-log and notification-types list the directory and read every migration; stretch, teacher-day, timplan-coverage, huvudman-reads, teacher-work-rules and sign-in/dto each name one), scripts/test/rls-policies.sql and generate-rls-area-matrix.ts and web/lib/admin-areas.ts (admin-areas: the web's copy of the matrix, and the block generated into the RLS suite), web/messages/{sv,en}.json (access-log, notification-types, staffing-checks), web/i18n/__fixtures__/engine-messages.json (staffing-checks, catalogue-sentences), and one file each for access-log, notification-types, sign-in/dto and ss12000-v2/attendance. Stryker runs only the specs that import a mutated file (jest.enableFindRelatedTests), so a spec that reads files but imports none, product-name.spec.ts, needs no entry. The specs stay in the run: each holds a mutant in src/ against a file outside it. Find the next missing entry with `npx stryker run --dryRunOnly`, which names the path. A bracket in a path is escaped, because the patterns are globs.
mutate_comment: Mutated is what a unit spec can observe, because unit specs are all Stryker runs (jest.mutation.config.js: src/**/*.spec.ts, never test/*.e2e-spec.ts). Left out on that principle, not by score. Bootstrap and wiring that only exists once Nest has built the application: main.ts, *.module.ts, and common/http-defaults.ts, which hands constant body-parser limits to the live Express instance and is proven by test/payload-limits.e2e-spec.ts. Controllers: their contract (route, guards, pipes, status code, throttling) lives in the request pipeline the e2e suite drives, so a unit spec calling a handler as a plain method skips exactly what makes it a controller; logic a controller grows belongs in a service, where it is mutated. auth/decorators: SetMetadata and createParamDecorator wrappers whose only output is metadata the guards read inside that pipeline. Anything that decides something stays in even while no spec reaches it: the guards, realtime/cors-io.adapter.ts (allowlist or no origin), config/configuration.ts (a pure function of the environment), the event names in realtime.types.ts, subjects.service.ts. The dto/, interfaces/ and enums/ exclusions predate this note and are not argued by it. Generated files (*.generated.ts) are left out too: src/integration/ss12000-v2/s1-provider.generated.ts is S1's OpenAPI schemas and parameter lists as a data module, 3,225 of the API's 73,861 mutants, and a mutant in it changes what the generator wrote, not anything a test of the gateway holds to account. Which of the rest is mutated on a given night is scripts/mutation-slice.mjs's business: it reads this list and deals the files into slices.
timeoutMS_comment: How long a mutant may run beyond 1.5 times the net time of the tests that cover it, before Stryker calls it a Timeout (which counts as detected). 60 s killed the runner, so it is 10 s, and the limit is a memory guard more than a time limit: do not raise it. On 2026-11-02 the slice that held src/notifications/notification-delivery.service.ts ended four times at the same mutant with 'The runner has received a shutdown signal'; bisecting by line range on CI narrowed it to the 14 mutants wholly inside lines 201-215 of that file (run 41554633962), where the job died with 60 s, with one worker, with a 1 GB heap and with two workers, and went through in about a minute with 8 s and 3 s. The mechanism was found afterwards by running the mutants against that file's digest test: `if (notice.userId !== target.user_id) continue;` on line 213, turned into `if (false) continue;` (and `===`), makes push() build a message for every pair of recipient and notice, 1,203 x 1,203, about 1.45 million messages and their formatted text, in a test of a whole-school digest. On a laptop that was 3,352 MiB after 5 s and 7,089 MiB after 10 s, outside V8's heap limit, which is why a 1 GB or 3 GB heap cap did nothing; no network is reached, the transport is mocked. Four workers and two such mutants side by side are more than a 16 GB runner holds, and the limit has to end the process before they get there. The square has since been taken out of the code (push() finds a person's notices by the person instead of comparing every device with every notice of the group, which was also quadratic in a real digest: 13.8 s against 3.4 s for 20,000 people with two devices each), so that mutant no longer exists. The 34 mutants wholly inside lines 186-232, where the old lines were, ran in 130 s on one worker with the process group at 1,556 MiB at most and a limit of 10 s, and with the same statuses (30 killed, 1 timed out, 2 survived, 1 not covered) in 141 s at 1,427 MiB with a limit of 60 s; the one Timeout is a mutant that loops, `at -= RECIPIENT_CHUNK`, which does not grow the process past those figures even in 60 s. A Timeout is detected, so a shorter limit can raise a score and not lower it, and it shortens the slices, whose seconds in scripts/mutation-slices.json were measured at 60 s; only slices 0, 2, 11 and 15 and the nine files of slice 14 have been run at 10 s. The limit could be raised again for this file's sake and is left at 10 s: a raise lengthens every night (the 155 timeouts of 60 s are some 130 minutes of worker time over the whole API) and gains no score, and a mutant that loops allocates until the limit ends it.
